data.caption: upairy.com
data.copy:
Only 4% of 2-year-olds in America are fully potty trained today.

But in the 1950s, that number was nearly 100%.

What changed? Disposable diapers.

And I'm sitting here absolutely furious because I've been buying diapers for my 3-year-old when kids her age used to be trained for over a year already.

—

So for the past 10 months everyone kept telling me "just wait until she's ready."

My pediatrician gave me this whole list of readiness signs to watch for.

Stays dry for 2 hours, shows interest in the potty, can pull pants up and down.

So I waited and watched while she stayed in diapers.

And every few weeks I'd think "okay maybe she's ready now?"

But there was always something holding me back from trying so I'd tell myself just wait a little longer.

Month after month after month.

Meanwhile she's 3 years old and my neighbor's 2-year-old daughter is already trained.

And I'd think "what am I doing wrong?"

But everyone said don't rush it, she'll tell you when she's ready.

So I kept waiting.

For 10 months.

—

So last week I was scrolling Reddit looking for advice.

And I saw this comment:

"Only 4% of American 2-year-olds are fully potty trained today. But in the 1950s, over 95% of kids were trained by 24 months."

Then: "By 1999, that 95% had dropped to 4%. That's not a typo. We went from nearly all kids trained by age 2 to almost none."

And I'm staring at my phone thinking... wait, WHAT?

My daughter is 36 months old and I'm being told to wait for readiness.

But in the 1950s, kids her age had been trained for over a year?

So I kept reading and the next line actually pissed me off.

"The shift happened because of disposable diapers. They were introduced in 1961."

"Within 40 years, the percentage of 2-year-olds trained dropped from 95% to 4%."

Like an entire generation of kids staying in diapers longer because of a product?

And I've been sitting here waiting for readiness for 10 months while the diapers were the problem the whole time?

So I went dow…

data.caption: trysaphire.com
data.copy:
My 9yr old still wets the bed. He stuffed his wet pull-up under his pillow last night and didn't tell me.

I found it this morning when I was making his bed. His pillows were soaked.

He was downstairs eating breakfast. Didn't say a word.

Here's the thing. He has dry nights sometimes. Maybe one or two a week.

And on those mornings he comes downstairs different. Lighter.

He'll tell me before I even ask. Big smile. "Mum, I was dry last night."

And I make a big deal of it. Of course I do. Because I know to reward him for the dry nights.

But the wet nights? He doesn't tell me about those. He hides the pull-up. Under the pillow. In his wardrobe.

One time he rolled it inside a pair of jeans at the bottom of his laundry basket.

He doesn't do it cause I make him feel bad about it. I haven't. I've read every article. I know not to shame him. I know it's not his fault.

But he's nine. And he knows his friends don't wear pull-ups to bed.

And somewhere along the way he decided that if I didn't see it, maybe it didn't happen.

But a few weeks ago his best friend's mom stopped me at school pickup.

"We should do a sleepover. We've never done one before. The boys would love it. C'mon, what's the harm?"

I smiled and said we'd organise something soon and I watched her walk away. I just stood there.

"What's the harm."

I couldn't explain it. I can't explain it to anyone who hasn't lived it.

The stress of a sleepover when your nine year old still wets the bed every night.

They're humiliating for him. The pull-up. The wet sleeping bag. Someone noticing. Someone saying something.

He came home from school the week before that in tears.

A boy in his class had invited him to a birthday sleepover. Everyone was going. He'd had to say no.

I asked him why he was crying and he looked at me and said something I haven't been able to stop thinking about.

"Momma. Why doesn't my body work like my friends?"

I didn't have an answer. I hugged him and told him his body was perfect.

data.caption: kittysupps.com
data.copy:
I lost my cat. Then I lost my job. Then I lost my boyfriend.

All because I thought a cough was a hairball.

If your cat gets low to the ground, extends their neck, and does that violent heaving cough where nothing comes up, please stop scrolling.

I know you think it's normal. I thought so too. For two years. I watched my cat do it once a month and said "come on buddy, get it up."

He's gone now. And I will never forgive myself for not knowing what I'm about to tell you.

My name is Anna Rodriguez. I'm 42. I live in San Antonio.

Three years ago, I had three cats: Simba, Milo, and Star.

Now I only have two.

And I almost lost them too.

Let me tell you what happened.

Because if your cat coughs and nothing comes up, you need to read this.

It started with Simba.

He was 8 years old. A big orange tabby. My best friend.

And once a month, like clockwork, he'd do this thing.

He'd get low to the ground. Extend his neck. And start this violent, rhythmic coughing.

His whole body would heave.

I'd sit there watching him, rubbing his back, saying "come on buddy, get it up."

Sometimes a hairball would come out.

Most of the time, nothing.

I assumed he was just trying. That it would come up eventually.

My mom said her cats did the same thing. "It's just hairballs. Cats do that."

So I didn't worry about it.

I bought those petroleum hairball gels from PetSmart. The ones that are supposed to help things slide through.

Didn't help.

I tried different foods. Different brushes. Different litters.

Nothing changed.

And then one night in November, three years ago, Simba collapsed.

He was breathing so hard his sides were heaving. His mouth was open. His tongue was blue.

I rushed him to the emergency vet.

They took him back immediately.

Thirty minutes later, the vet came out.

"He's in respiratory distress. We need to do chest X-rays, bloodwork, and get him on oxygen. It's going to be about $1,400."

I didn't have $1,400.

But I told them to do it anyway.

data.caption: Why my crown kept thinning on every oil
data.copy:
My seven-year-old asked why I never wear my hair like Jaylen's mom.

Alopecia. Nineteen years of it.

I had bald patches on my crown. My own son had never seen them.

I turned around to the sink and ran the water so he couldn't see my face.

That night I put the $48 bottle in the trash under coffee grounds so nobody would ask.

Around $3,600 on oils, treatments and salon appointments. Then 365 days of a multivitamin with no difference.

Every single thing I bought was somebody selling me something to rub on the outside of a scalp that had already quit on the inside — the oils, the salon treatments, the pills, all the same thing in a different bottle with a different price on it.

My son has been looking at my head longer than my husband has, and he's the only one who ever said anything out loud.

That he grows up remembering me as the mom who was hiding something, and being embarrassed for me before he's old enough to understand why.

I decided I'm done getting up at 5:40 to fix it before the house wakes up — Saturday I'm going to sit in my cousin's kitchen and let her put the light right on it and tell me the truth about what's left.

There was a cause nobody had ever told me about called Sleeping Follicles.

I'll tell you what that means. I have to go back to the year I noticed my husband had stopped putting his hand on the back of my head first, or none of it will make sense.

========

I did everything the labels told me to do.

I kept every morning and every night.

I made every visit.

I paid every bill.

The pictures stayed the same.

Not one hair came back.

========

I bought thick castor oil because something that heavy felt like it had to stay and work.

Then batana, rosemary oil, and every growth serum took the next Sunday.

Nine years and more than $1,800 later, the crown still shone.

========

Edge control and gel made sense because a flat front meant nobody had to know.

data.copy:
I am BEGGING you.

If your dog keeps getting hot spots that come back somewhere different every three weeks, don't you DARE scroll past this post.

Don't you dare tell yourself "it's just a food allergy." Don't you dare listen to your vet saying "some dogs are just atopic." Don't you dare switch to the salmon formula and think you handled it.

I did all of that. Every single thing. For two years.

My dog is gone right now.

He was 9. He was healthy. He was my best friend. And he died from resistant secondary infections on top of a skin barrier that had been failing for two years while I kept switching his food.

I'm $11,000 in debt. I spent thousands on prescription food and Apoquel and vet rechecks and medicated shampoos. My husband and I fought constantly about the money. I moved Chester into the bedroom so I could hear him scratch at night.

And if one random errand to a rescue hadn't changed everything, I'd have lost another dog instead of one.

You have five minutes. That's all this takes. Five minutes to read what happened to me. And it might be the only reason your dog is still alive a year from now.

My name is Mary Rooney. I'm 44. I live in Denver, Colorado.

Three years ago, I had three dogs: Max, Scout, and Luna.

Now I only have two.

And I almost lost them too.

Let me tell you what happened.

Because if your dog's hot spots keep relocating to new locations every three weeks, you need to read this.

It started with Max.

He was 9 years old. A big soft Golden Retriever. My best friend.

And once a month, like clockwork, he'd get a new hot spot.

A different location every time. His belly. Then behind his left ear. Then his lower back. Then the backs of his legs.

I'd sit there treating each one. "Come on, let's get this cleared."

Sometimes it cleared quickly.

Most of the time, it cleared for two weeks and came back somewhere new.

I assumed we just hadn't found the right protein yet. That it would resolve eventually.

data.caption: shophealthypetz.com
data.copy:
people keep asking me what i did and i finally have time to write it out properly. before and after of my boy below.

first pic is from the worst of it — january this year. i'd been crying in the bath after putting him to bed because i didn't know what else to try. he was on apoquel + cytopoint + prescription food + medicated shampoo + ear cleaner every other day. about $400 a month. he was still scratching all night every night.

second pic is from this week.

i'd posted his before pic in here back in january asking if anyone had any ideas. honestly nothing anyone suggested ended up working. raw food. grain free. fish oil. probiotic chews. allergy shots. shampoo rotations. tried all of it. nothing held longer than a couple weeks.

what finally worked was a liquid collagen supplement. specifically for rebuilding the skin barrier, which apparently is the actual structural problem behind chronic allergies and nobody had ever explained that to me in 4 years of vet visits.

the way it was explained to me — the skin barrier is a wall made of collagen. when it breaks down (which happens progressively after age 2 in most dogs because they lose collagen with age), allergens penetrate the skin and the immune system reacts. that reaction is everything — the scratching, the ears, the paws, the hot spots, the rust staining. apoquel suppresses the reaction but doesn't repair the wall. so the wall keeps degrading underneath and the medication has to work harder and harder. that's why the doses climb. that's why nothing ever holds.

most collagen for dogs products are type 1 only in chew form which can't actually rebuild the barrier no matter how long you give them. the one i ended up trying has all 3 collagen types in liquid hydrolyzed form with the cofactors the body needs to assemble the collagen into new barrier tissue. that's the difference. and apparently that's why most people in this group have said collagen doesn't work — they tried products that couldn't possibly…

data.caption: try.oviaessentials.com
data.copy:
My husband left me in March for a 29 year old. Two weeks ago he texted me asking if he could come home. 

I've been debating posting this for about two weeks. 

Four different people have asked me what I did and I'm tired of typing it out one at a time, so I'm just going to put the whole thing here. 

It's long. Sorry. I'm not a writer and my daughter is going to be mortified.

Last March I came home early on a Tuesday and heard the shower running upstairs at two in the afternoon. I'll spare you the rest of it. 

I didn't scream at anyone, I just closed the door and went back downstairs and sat at the kitchen table until it got dark, which sounds dramatic but I genuinely did not know what else to do.

That night I stood in the bathroom and looked at myself properly for the first time in about three years. 

I'd been avoiding mirrors for far longer than I’d like to admit. 

Perimenopause hit me at 47 and never let up.

40 pounds in two years and I did not change one thing about how I ate.

My stomach sat on top of my jeans no matter what I bought. 

My face was puffy every single morning. 

My jaw had sort of melted into my neck. 

My skin was gray under that bathroom light.

And I was hungry all the time. I'd eat a full dinner and be hungry again by 8. 

I'd stand in the kitchen at 9pm eating out of the fridge without even being hungry, just doing it, then hating myself while I did it. 

I thought about food all day. Every day. It never shut off.

Standing there that night, I understood why he did it. 

That's an awful thing to admit and I know how it sounds but it's the truth. I didn't recognize her either.

I'd tried everything for three years. 

Counted every calorie for eight straight months. 10,000 steps a day. 

Pilates four times a week and then cardio on top when Pilates stopped doing anything. 

Apple cider vinegar gummies. Magnesium. Those berberine capsules everyone talks about, I took those for two months (about $40 down the drain).

Nothing moved. Not…

data.caption: upairy.com
data.copy:
In Vietnam, the average age of potty training is 9 months old. (I promise I’m not making this up - it’s a documented cultural norm) 

In the US, it has crept up to 36+ months. 

Are American babies biologically different? No. 

Are Vietnamese moms wizards? No. 

The difference is simply what we wrap our kids butts in. 

And I sat there staring at these stats, realizing I was 2 years behind a standard I didn't even know existed.

—

So for the past 14 months everyone kept telling me "wait until she's ready."

My pediatrician gave me this whole checklist of readiness signs to watch for.

Stays dry for 2 hours, shows interest in the potty, can follow simple instructions.

So I waited and watched while she stayed in pull-ups.

And every few weeks I'd think "okay maybe she's ready now?"

But there was always one sign missing so I'd tell myself just wait a little longer.

Month after month after month.

Meanwhile she's 3 and a half and I'm watching 2-year-olds at the playground already trained.

And I'd think "what am I doing wrong?"

But everyone said don't rush it, she'll tell you when she's ready.

So I kept waiting.

For 14 months.

While she stayed comfortable in disposables that I changed 6 times a day.

—

So last week I was scrolling Reddit at 11 PM trying to figure out how the heck they do it so early. 

And I saw this comment that connected the dots for me. 

It turns out, we used to be almost as fast as them.

"92% of children in 1957 were toilet trained by 18 months." 

Then: "The current average is 35 months for girls, 39 months for boys." 

And I'm staring at my phone thinking... wait, WHAT? 

So the US used to be like Vietnam, but now we're 2 years behind?

So I went down a complete rabbit hole that night. 

I found data from the American Academy of Family Physicians. 

In the 1940s, we were training almost as early as they do in Vietnam. 

Now it starts between 21 and 36 months.

And only 40 to 60 percent of kids even COMPLETE training by 36 months…

data.caption: upairy.com
data.copy:
Only 16% of mothers with young children worked outside the home in the 1950s. Today it's 70%.

And everyone's right—we don't have time to potty train the way they did back then.

Which is why 92% of children in 1957 were potty trained by 18 months.

I work 45 hours a week. I have maybe 3 hours with my daughter on weeknights after pickup.

So I kept delaying. 

"I'll start when I have more time." 
"I'll wait until she's older." 
"I need days off work to do this right."

And now she's 4 years old. Still in diapers. And I'm sitting here absolutely furious.

—

My name is Bec. I'm 31 years old. I work full-time in marketing.

For the past 2 years, everyone kept telling me 

"you need to take time off work to potty train."

"You need 3-5 days straight at home with no interruptions."

"Working moms can't do this the same way stay-at-home moms can."

So I kept waiting for the "right time."

Waiting for a week off. Waiting for her to get older so it would be faster. Waiting for it to somehow get easier.

Meanwhile she turned 3. Then 3 and a half. Then 4.

And I kept thinking "when I have time off work, we'll do it then."

But I never had that time.

And last month, my mother-in-law came over for dinner.

She watched me change my daughter's diaper after bath time.

"You know, in my day, mothers stayed home. My kids were all trained by 18 months."

She didn't say it mean. Just... matter-of-fact.

Like of course I'm struggling. I work. Husband doesn't really help. What did I expect?

Because she's right, isn't she?

If I'd stayed home like my mom did. Like her mom did. Like 84% of moms did in the 1950s.

Maybe this wouldn't be so hard.

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.
countries.notes: MX/CO/CL are not in this Meta targeting catalog. Use store_based_in for stores based in those markets.

excludeCountries.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.

KB Back In Stock Restock Alert
Sticky Add To Cart Booster Pro
POWR Email Popup Sales Pop Ups
EG Auto Add to Cart Free Gift
SA Request a Quote, Hide Price
Zoorix Sticky Add To Cart Bar
Tada Pop up Spin Wheel Popups
Coupon X: Discount Code Pop Up
SC Back in Stock Restock Alert

mcp_pagination.hint: Pass scroll_next as scroll on the next call with the same filters to continue. Do not rely on page alone.
